## About this course {.unnumbered}

Ecologists want to understand why nature works the way it does. Does rainfall reduce foraging opportunities? Does predation cause reproductive failure? Answering such questions requires far more than fitting statistical models. It requires thinking carefully and deliberately about causality. This course takes a causal-first approach to messy ecological data. Students will learn to formulate logical hypotheses of different types, generate estimand-aware predictions that clearly identify effects that they actually want to learn about. Students then use Structural Causal Models (SCMs) and Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs) to represent ecological knowledge, eplicitly state causal assumptions (based on evidence), and determine whether those effects can be identified from data. Rather than letting AIC decide which variables matter (or assuming that fitting a Structural Equation Model (SEM) makes an analysis causal, or letting the traditional SEM approach quietly eliminate causal assumptions), students will learn to clearly and quickly distinguish between causal reasoning from statistical machinery. Using their own projects (and recently discovered and absolutely real long-term datasets on jackalope ecology), students will then conduct their own analyses.

## **AI usage transparency** {.unnumbered}

In the construction of this website, GenAI (via ChatGPT) was used in the following ways:

* **Generating graphics of cryptid jackalope species.** This was part of an exercise in prompt engineering—specifically, learning how to design minimalist prompts that produce consistent visual themes across all outputs.

* **Converting the Canvas-based course site into Quarto markdown.** This included restructuring content, standardizing headers, and translating existing materials into a reproducible, version-controlled format (for hosting on GitHub).

* **Assistive learning of custom CSS**, in parallel with consulting online CSS documentation and manuals (i.e., as a tutor and debugger, not a design authority).

* **Reformatting and updating existing tables**, including updating of revised dates, assignments, and course logistics.

* **Error-checking and troubleshooting markdown and Quarto code.** This was necessary during site builds.

* **Improving organization across course components.** This included suggestions for cross-referencing related pages and identifying places where additional examples or clarifications would improve learning outcomes.

* **Evaluating pedagogical alignment.** This involved getting feedback on readability, cognitive load, and whether learning objectives were being met by the material being presented.

* **Editorial support** to ensure that tone and level of explanatory detail was appropriate for graduate students. This included tightening some language and reducing informational redundancy across pages.

GenAI was used as an assistive tool throughout; it was not used as a content authority, decision-maker, or substitute for subject-matter expertise. All instructional choices, interpretations, and final edits remain the responsibility of the instructor (in accordance with [AI Use Policy](../chapters/int_ai_policy.qmd)).
:::
